zones.label: Column 1

Consulted after independent scan reading; its readings do not determine this copy's typography. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Sataguai is equated with Satano foca, beyond ordinary discussion. The headword also resolves the worn catchword on the preceding page; the Portuguese fa- continues as falar.

runs.text: lar, &c. Palaura pera encarecer algũa couſa

lines.note: Completes falar and explains an emphatic expression about something badly done. Restored the missing l in Palaura from its visible ascender; encarecer here means to emphasize, not simply to raise a price.
Specifies that the thing being emphasized is badly done. This short continuation closes Sataguai and is not a separate entry.
The reader is referred to Sata, where the preceding page defines a judge or person hearing the parties. Sata is printed in roman type after italic Vide.
This cross-reference likewise points to Sata. Corrected the OCR's typeface split inside Sata: the whole reference word is upright, while Vide is italic.
Satçuqi and Goguachi name the fifth lunar month. The historical syllable spellings and nasal abbreviation lũa are preserved without substituting a modern calendar month.
Satçuqiame and Samidare denote the rains of the fifth month. They are headword and synonym, not embedded Portuguese terms; quin- continues below.
Completes quin-to and the lunar-month definition of the rains. Both mes and lũa belong to the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Palaura que ſerue pera ſaudar. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Sate is first described as a word used in greeting. The paragraph sign and Item introduce further senses within the same entry.

runs.text: Interjeição em couſas de admiração. ¶ Item,

lines.note: A second use of Sate is an interjection expressing surprise. The final Item leads directly to the temporal connective sense below.
The final sense is after that or then. The source's beta-shaped double-s sort in dißo is retained.

runs.text: Interjeição do que ſe admira, ou cõ-

lines.note: Satecoso is used by someone expressing wonder or conceding something. The damaged rounded letter in the headword agrees with co; the Portuguese cõ- abbreviation continues as concede.
Completes the concession sense of the preceding interjection. The nasal stroke in algũa is visible and retained.
Read Satemata rather than Satomata: the worn fourth letter has an open e form, and the entry belongs to the Sate series. The gloss is again or moreover.
Satemo is an exclamation of astonishment. The Japanese word is distinct from the italic Portuguese definition.
The repeated form Satemosatemo has the same astonished use as Satemo. The central long s is printed as part of a single headword.
Corrected Sateſare to Sateſate: the second repeated element has a t with a short cross-stroke. Besides the preceding exclamatory sense, the entry introduces a greeting or welcome.
Completes ſau-dação and the welcoming sense of Satesate. The historical agaſalhado is retained as printed.
Sateua is rendered as Is that so? Enlarged comparison with aßi below shows a double-s sort, represented here as ß, rather than the OCR's single ſ; the question mark remains.

Restored the headword's capital S, misread as B. This Satǒ is associated with Fidarimichi and Bocuxôno gui and is explained below in terms of poverty or inadequacy; it is distinct from the later sugar entry. The two long-o marks differ visibly, ǒ and ô.

runs.text: breza, ou pouquidade. Item, Couſa deſpro-

lines.note: Completes Po-breza and adds scantiness, then something disproportionate. Corrected Corſa to Couſa and the false terminal s to the visible line-end hyphen in deſpro-.

runs.text: porcionada, ou que não quadra com a qualidade

lines.note: Completes deſpro-porcionada and describes something inappropriate to a person's quality or standing. The following row completes that social comparison.

The example begins Satǒno sama tarito, referring to an inadequate appearance or condition. The Portuguese estado retains the supplied st representation pending the separate ligature audit; no blanket long-s substitution is made.

The Japanese concessive example continues with iyedomo and iteino catachiuo mote, contrasting an unsuitable appearance with an unusual form. The complete &c. is italic, not split between fonts. Poſ begins the Portuguese concession without a supplied terminal hyphen.

runs.text: to que otrajo emaneira não era qual deuia ſer, to-

lines.note: Completes Poſ-to and says that the dress and manner were not as they should have been. The tight source groups otrajo and emaneira are retained; to- begins todauia below.

runs.text: dauia com trajo, ou figura extra ordinaria, &c.

lines.note: Corrected dauta to dauia, completing todauia, nevertheless. The clause describes extraordinary dress or appearance; extra ordinaria remains separated as in the supplied source-aligned text.
A second example offers something despite its poor or scant nature. Satǒnigozaredomo is printed as a joined group; ma- continues as mama on the next line.

runs.text: Poſto q̃ he couſa pobre & pou

lines.note: Completes the humble offering formula. Corrected Peſto and pabre to Poſto and pobre from the rounded worn vowels; q̃ remains abbreviated. The final pou has no visible hyphen and continues as pouca.

runs.text: ca, aßi como a achei, ou veo a offereço a v. m.

lines.note: Completes pou-ca: although the offering is poor and small, it is presented as found or received. The historical veo and the courtesy abbreviation v. m. are not expanded.
Unaccented Sato denotes a village or settlement. The worn last round vowel of pouoação was misread as e; restored o without changing the historical u/v spelling.

This accented Satǒ means sugar or jaggery. Read ou jagra rather than the OCR cujagra: the first round vowel is open through wear, and the visible gap precedes jagra. The damaged o is a nonblocking uncertainty; the gloss is not silently changed to a modern sugar term.
Satoi describes someone of penetrating, subtle intelligence. Enlarging Peßoa shows the same double-s sort as aßi, not the OCR's single ſ; delgado is retained in its figurative sense.

runs.text: que logo penetra as couſas. Vt,

lines.note: The definition describes immediately grasping things; Satoifito illustrates a perceptive person. The Japanese example is printed as one group, which is retained.

runs.text: Lugar, ou pouoação cercada à roda

lines.note: Satojǒ is a settlement surrounded by a defensive enclosure. Restored the damaged letters in pouoação, which OCR rendered poucação; the headword's final o has a caron.

runs.text: como fortaleza, ou fortaleza que eſtà ao pee

lines.note: The definition also includes a fortress at the foot of a hill. Two e forms are visible in pee at the right edge; the OCR's single pe omitted the second.

runs.text: de algum monte, ou fortaleza alta.

lines.note: Completes the mountain-foot description and adds a high fortress. This is still the Satojǒ explanation, not a separate topographical entry.

The sugar buns are described as small rolls cooked by steam. Corrected the OCR's initial f in fèozinhos to the descending p, but retained the locally read èo in pèozinhos: the worn mark looks grave-like, and the print does not securely support normalizing it to pãezinhos. This is a nonblocking spelling/diacritic uncertainty. The unusual hyphen after com is visibly printed.

runs.text: o bafo dagoa quente feitos com aſucar.

lines.note: The rolls are cooked in the vapor of hot water and made with sugar. The source's joined dagoa and historical aſucar are retained.

runs.text: Mochis feitos com jagra, ou a-

lines.note: Satǒmochi are mochi containing jaggery or sugar. Restored Mochis, feitos and com from the OCR's Mechis, ſeitos and cem; the f in feitos is meaningful, not a long-s variant. Mochis is Japanese-derived vocabulary inside the Portuguese definition.
Completes a-ſucar and specifies the sweet filling inside. The short row belongs to Satǒmochi.

runs.text: Meloẽs doces, ou de bom ſabor.

lines.note: Satǒvri denotes sweet or good-tasting melons. Enlarging the worn noun reveals a faint o before the marked e: read Meloẽs, not Melẽs, and keep the tilde on e rather than shifting it to modern Melões.

Satori is explained as divining or arriving at the correct understanding. The inflection otta agrees with the printed rounded vowel and the supplied lexical index. The source-aligned spacing a certar is retained rather than normalized automatically.

runs.text: a couſa que ſe cuida, ou imagina.

lines.note: Completes the verb's explanation: getting right what one considers or imagines. The damaged o forms are interpreted within otherwise legible couſa and imagina.

runs.text: O adeuinhar, ou a certar com o que

lines.note: The noun Satori repeats the act of divining or understanding correctly. Its Portuguese explanation parallels the preceding verb, including the retained a certar spacing.

runs.text: ſe cuida, ou imagina. ¶ Item, Modo de

lines.note: The ordinary understanding sense ends here; Item introduces the religious sense on the next line. The paragraph sign is not part of the Japanese word.

runs.text: meditar dos Ienxus, & cair nas couſas do Bup

lines.note: Corrected moditar to meditar. The text describes the meditation of Ienxus and insight into Buddhist matters; Ienxus and Bup occur inside Portuguese prose. Only Bup is legible at the right edge, with no secure continuation or final punctuation, so an expected longer Buppǒ is not supplied. The broken left rule is not an omitted text row.

Restored the severely worn Satǒyǒcan, sugar yōkan, and the Portuguese description of sweet slices. Both o marks open upward; the NINJAL entry confirms the lexical identity but not the impression. At the right edge only faze is recoverable: no secure final m or nasal stroke is visible, so the expected fazem is not silently supplied. These damaged readings remain nonblocking uncertainties.

The slices are made of beans and sugar. Recovered the entire italic Portuguese row from garbled mixed-font OCR; the tilde is over the e in feijoẽs, not over the preceding o. Lowercase aſucar follows the ampersand in the scan.
Saua is the adverb thus or so. The example begins Chijnno nacani, among intimate friends, and divides sa-ua across the next row; the grammatical label and Portuguese gloss are italic.
Completes the assertion that such a thing is not found among friends. Corrected ba to ha from the h ascender in the Portuguese phrase não ha.

runs.text: tal couſa. i, Ser aßi desleal, &c.

lines.note: The explanation specifies that the absent conduct is being so disloyal. The source-aligned short s in desleal is retained; i, introduces an explanatory restatement here.

runs.text: Preſa, ou tanque de agoa, q̃ ſẽpre corre.

lines.note: This different Saua denotes a reservoir or pool with continually flowing water. Restored the second r in corre from the two printed strokes; q̃ and ſẽpre remain abbreviated.

runs.text: Borda deſta preſa, ou tanque de agoa

lines.note: Sauabe is the edge of the pool just defined. The Portuguese demonstrative links this compound to the preceding Saua entry.
The retained water comes from the mountains. Corrected monter to montes: the final glyph is a short s, not r.
Sauagaxi means to disturb or cause disorder. The historical past ending aita is retained. At the right edge the OCR as is actually a followed by a hyphen, continuing auer below.
Completes a-uer reuoltas, to cause disturbances. The Japanese example begins with the capital-city area as object and divides the verb saua- across rows.
Completes sauagasumajiqi tameni, so as not to disturb, and places the lodging outside the capital. The historical racuguai spelling is retained rather than modernized.
The example takes lodging outside Miaco. Mia- is the first part of a Japanese place-name embedded in the Portuguese translation; the printed hyphen remains.

runs.text: co pera que não cauſaſe perturbação dẽtro.

lines.note: Completes Mia-co and explains avoiding disturbance inside the city. The nasal abbreviation dẽtro and supplied single-s form cauſaſe are retained from this impression.

runs.text: Couſa de em barulhada, ou pertur-

lines.note: Sauagaxij concerns tumult or disturbance. Corrected the vowel in pertur- from the OCR pertar-; the unusual source wording de em barulhada and its spacing are retained instead of being rewritten as ordinary modern Portuguese.
Completes pertur-bação and adds the state of being disturbed. The provisional eſtar ligature representation is kept without a global s/ſ reclassification.
This indented noun is the -sa derivative of Sauagaxij, the quality of disturbance or noisiness. The absence of a separate Portuguese gloss is genuine.
This indented form is the adverbial derivative of Sauagaxij. Its u carries a clearly downward-opening circumflex, not a caron.
Sauagui is the intransitive counterpart, becoming disturbed or there being an uproar. The final rebo- continues into the next row.
Completes rebo-liço, commotion or uproar, from the preceding verb definition. The cedilla is preserved in this short body row.
The noun names disturbance or revolt. Corrected Pertarbação to Perturbação from the u strokes, consistent with the same noun elsewhere on the page.

runs.text: Esfregão feito de bam bus partidos, &

lines.note: Sauara is a scrubber made of split bamboo. Corrected Etfregão to Esfregão, whose short s is visible before f, and partides to partidos. The supplied internal spacing bam bus is retained rather than normalized on lexical grounds alone.

runs.text: juntos pera roçar, ou eſfregar algũa couſa.

lines.note: The split pieces are gathered together for scraping or rubbing something. This explains the construction of the scrubber, not a separate bamboo species.
Nauazauara is the corresponding scrubber made of ropes. It is a Japanese subentry with its own gloss, not a Japanese word embedded inside the Portuguese sentence.
A separate homograph names a fish, glossed by the historical Portuguese peixe serra. No modern species identification is imposed on this brief definition.
Sauari means meeting or coming into contact with something. The nasal abbreviation in nalgũa is visible, and the Portuguese object continues below.
The example says that a fish touched the hand. Vuoga is the historical spelling of fish with the subject particle; the Portuguese pei- is divided at the right edge.
Completes pei-xe and the sentence a fish touched my hand. The tilde remains over a in mão.
This noun means an impediment or obstruction. The abbreviation Impedimẽto is retained without expanding the omitted nasal consonant.

Read Sauariuo, not Sauarino: enlargement shows an open-topped u after ri, forming the object particle uo. The phrase means to cause an obstruction. Also corrected eſteruo to eſtoruo from the rounded vowel.
Saua yacana is equated with Qireina and describes something clean or polished. The printed space within the headword is retained; limpa begins with an l, not the OCR t.
The definition adds lustrous or polished and gives an example of a person with delicate hands and feet. The Japanese illustration is a standalone sentence, not a typeface-term annotation target.

runs.text: Homem de mãos, & pès delicados, & poli-

lines.note: The example is translated as a person with refined, polished hands and feet. Corrected terminal polr to poli- from the dotted i and visible hyphen at the curved right edge.

Completes poli-dos, then gives a cleanly arranged feast as another example. Enlarging the curved gutter resolves the OCR Conuis as Conuite; its final te is compressed but present, and the word is not divided onto the next row.
The feast is clean and well prepared. This row supplies the adjectives modifying the complete Conuite on the preceding line.
This indented derivative is the adverb corresponding to Saua yacana. The complete grammatical abbreviation Adu. is italic; no missing definition is inferred.
The -sa noun gives the quality described by Saua yacana. Its indentation and lack of a separate Portuguese gloss match the related derivative above.
Sauo is a bamboo pole used for hanging clothes. The source's dependurão and unpunctuated final &c are retained; the last character lies close to the curved column rule.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Vara com q̃ leuão a embarcação pel-

lines.note: Another sense is a pole used to move a boat along a river. Corrected the garbled pula to pel- from the visible p, e, l and terminal hyphen; the next row completes historical pello.
Completes pel-lo rio, along the river, in the boat-poling definition. The doubled l results from the actual line division and is not simplified.
Sauogana is a long iron tool used by carpenters for planing. Restored the gutter-compressed h and final o in acepilhão, which the OCR reduced to acepilãs; the nasal mark remains over a.
Identifies carpenters as the users of the long planing iron. The subject follows the verb on the preceding row.
Sauorivobi is a kind of woven sash or belt. Corrected the terminal s in tecids to the compressed round o; the headword's historical vowel sequence is retained.
The woven belt is narrow and small. This short continuation completes Sauorivobi.
Sauoxica is a poetic term for a deer, equated with Xixi. The P. label is upright in this impression; the Japanese synonym is not marked as embedded Portuguese vocabulary.
Saxacu denotes a small tea spoon or scoop. Cha occurs inside the Portuguese noun phrase and is a whole-word typeface-review target.
The verb expresses causing someone to do something; the repeated fazer is intentional causative wording. The printed eta is retained rather than expanded from an expected paradigm.

Saxen denotes being exiled and is glossed by the Japanese passive Nagaſaruru. The final written-register label S. is upright, outside the italic Portuguese gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Corrected ſaxerari to ſaxeranu: the n/u strokes are worn, but enlargement, the negative-use explanation, and the NINJAL headword support the negative form. Restored f in defecti- and its visible line-end hyphen. The worn n remains a nonblocking glyph uncertainty.

runs.text: uo que ſempre ſe vſa no negatiuo, ou junto com

lines.note: Completes defecti-uo and says that the expression is used negatively or together with another element. Corrected corn to com from the final m strokes. The definition continues onto the next page; the separate lower-right algum is a catchword, not an added body continuation.

zones.label: Catchword
zones.note: The complete catchword reads algum in italic at the curved lower-right edge; no terminal punctuation is supplied.
